name: MarkupMarkdownTrendPhase
quote: Markup: The classic uptrend... Markdown: The downtrend that follows distribution.
description: Defines the other two cycle phases: markup is a sustained series of higher swing highs and higher swing lows (mirrored: markdown is lower swing highs and lower swing lows). The classic with-trend-legs-and-pullbacks structure Grimes references here ('a series of with-trend legs interspersed with pullbacks') is developed fully in Chapter 3 (mined separately); this candidate is the cycle-level phase test.
pseudocode: lastSwingHigh(1) > lastSwingHigh(2) AND lastSwingLow(1) > lastSwingLow(2)  // uses G01-01 pivot detection

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection (G01-01) and comparison of the two most recent pivot pairs

chapter_title: The Market Cycle and the Four Trades

name: AcceleratedTrendRate
quote: Note the classic signs of a buying climax in this example: an accelerated trend rate, large range bars
description: The rate of the trend (price change per bar) over a short recent window is a multiple of the rate over an equal, older window -- the trend is steepening.

complexity.reason: compares two lagged price-difference rates, no persistent state but two offset reads

notes: Grimes gives 'rate' no formula; this reduces price/time slope to a ratio of two displacement rates. Distance rather than magnitude, so sides is 'same' (abs()), unlike a directional momentum test.

name: SharpCountertrendMomentumBreaksTrend
quote: this pullback completely broke the established trend pattern, and spiked the MACD to a sharp new low, which is not consistent with an intact uptrend
description: A large-range bar against the trend direction during a pullback (mirrors G03-04, directional) -- the trend is considered broken; block further with-trend entries until a new impulse confirms the trend again. Same mechanics apply to the 'wrong side' pullback-failure pattern described later in the chapter (page 89-90).

complexity.reason: a window average plus a directional bar test

name: DowTrendChangeUncertainThenConfirmed
quote: if the market falls short of the previous pivot high, the trend status becomes uncertain ... The trend change is actually confirmed only when price trades through the last pivot low, marking a lower low
description: Trend status becomes 'uncertain' when a with-trend leg fails to make a new extreme past the prior pivot; the downtrend is only confirmed once price also breaks the last pivot low -- Dow theory's first trend-change pattern.
pseudocode: swingFailedToExceedPriorPivotHigh AND (state == UNCERTAIN) AND close[0] < priorPivotLow -> state = DOWNTREND

complexity.reason: a multi-stage pivot state machine (up / down / uncertain) needing a swing detector

name: HigherTimeframeTrendAlignmentFilter
quote: the uptrend on the daily chart is likely to terminate suddenly as the weekly chart reasserts control and the downtrend on that time frame resumes
description: Only take with-trend pullback entries on the trading timeframe when a higher-timeframe proxy (a much longer-lookback moving-average slope on the same bars) agrees in direction; avoid entries counter to that higher timeframe.

complexity.reason: 'higher time frame trend' is a genuine design decision even once approximated by a longer lookback -- how much longer, and how to reconcile conflicting timeframes, needs a choice by the authoring pass

notes: Higher timeframe approximated per the mining brief by a longer lookback on the same bars rather than a true multi-timeframe read.

name: PriceMostlyAboveMaTrendFilter
quote: when price spends a lot of time on one side of a moving average, this suggests the market is trending in that direction
description: Over the last lookback bars, at least fracThreshold of the closes are above (below, mirrored) an intermediate-length moving average; used as a with-trend context gate rather than a signal.
pseudocode: barsAbove(close, ema(close, maLength), lookback) >= fracThreshold * lookback

complexity.reason: a window loop counting closes on one side of a moving average over N bars

notes: Grimes does not commit to SMA vs EMA for this generic reference average in this chapter; EMA used as a default, type should be a switchable parameter.

Grimes explicitly says he does not use this mechanically, e.g. 'executing only at the precise points where the line shifts slopes'; recorded anyway as a codeable context filter per the high-recall directive.

name: MaSlopeTrendFilter
quote: Longer-term (100-period or more) moving averages will address longer-term trends, while very short-term (less than 10-period) moving averages will give indications for the shortest intervals on the chart.
description: The moving average of length maLength is higher now than slopeLookback bars ago (up-sloping), used as a with-trend context gate; mirrored for down-sloping/short context.

complexity.reason: needs a moving average and an offset comparison against its own prior value

notes: Grimes gives no exact bar count for measuring the slope; slopeLookback=5 is a chosen default, note in text.

Grimes explicitly warns this filter lags: 'the lag effect will cause you to miss many good trades at the beginning, but you will be green-lighted to take all the losers at the end of a trend.' Recorded anyway per high-recall directive; authoring pass should weigh this caveat.

name: HigherTimeframeTrendAlignmentFilter
quote: When a higher time frame is trending, patterns that work with that trend direction on lower time frames will be reinforced. Win rates will be higher, and moves will be sharper and cleaner... patterns that run contra to that trend on lower time frames will tend to abort.
description: Only allow a with-trend entry when a longer-lookback (htfMultiplier times the trading-timeframe length) moving average is also sloping in the trade's direction. Mirrored for shorts.
pseudocode: ema(close, maLength * htfMultiplier)[0] > ema(close, maLength * htfMultiplier)[htfSlopeLookback]

complexity.reason: same mechanic as the single-timeframe MA slope filter (G07-02), computed at a longer lookback

name: LowerTimeframeTippingPointTimingEntry
quote: This is what happens when the moderate and predictable momentum from a lower time frame break feeds into a structure that is already at the tipping point on a higher time frame... an alert trader could have used the tests of support and resistance on the higher time frames... to enter at the beginning of strong trends on the lower time frame.
description: Use a fast/short-lookback breakout (approximating a lower time frame than the trading time frame, i.e. a lookback divided by htfMultiplier) of a recent support/resistance test to time entries precisely into a bigger higher-time-frame-approximated pattern that is already at a structural tipping point.
pseudocode: close[0] > highest(high[1], round(rangeLookback / htfMultiplier)) && htfAtTippingPoint(rangeLookback * htfMultiplier)

complexity.reason: the fast breakout itself is a simple window-high check, but 'already at a structural tipping point on the higher time frame' needs a design decision (what counts as a tipping point: a range edge? a prior pivot?) before it is fully codeable

name: DailyLossLimitSwitch
quote: Is there a loss level at which you will stop trading for the day/week/month?
description: Equity lost since the start of the current calendar day (or week/month) exceeds a dollar threshold; blocks new entries and forces flat until the period rolls over. The daily-loss-limit generalization of the existing MonthlyProfitTarget Switch, mirrored onto the loss side and onto a day/week boundary instead of a fixed calendar month.

complexity.reason: needs a design decision for how the day/week/month boundary is detected and how starting equity is captured and held as persistent state across bars; the underlying comparison (equity change since a period start vs. a threshold) is simple once that plumbing exists, exactly as MonthlyProfitTarget already does for a calendar month

notes: Grimes gives no explicit dollar figure; the phrasing is a question the trader must answer for his own plan. dailyLossLimit = 1000 is an arbitrary placeholder default, flagged for calibration by the authoring pass.

MonthlyProfitTarget already gates entries on cumulative equity gain since the start of the calendar month (Switch role, blocks entries, forces flat); this candidate is its mirror image (loss instead of gain) generalized to day/week/month instead of a fixed month boundary.
EquityDrawdownFilter is close but reads a rolling N-bar lookback rather than resetting at a calendar boundary -- a different accessor pattern (variable history vs. a captured period-start value).

name: TradeCountLimitSwitch
quote: How many trades a day/week/month will you allow?
description: The number of entries already taken in the current calendar day (or week/month) reaches a cap; blocks further entries until the period rolls over.
pseudocode:
// tradesToday counts entries taken since the first bar of the current date
if (date[0] != date[1]) tradesToday = 0
if (ctx.MarketPosition() != 0 and ctx.BarsSinceEntry() == 0) tradesToday = tradesToday + 1
tradesToday >= maxTradesPerDay

complexity.reason: no existing ctx accessor counts entries taken since a period start; TotalTrades (used by LastTradeCooldown) is cumulative since the strategy began, not since the current day/week/month started, so a new persistent counter plus a day-boundary reset would need to be designed

notes: Grimes gives no explicit cap; maxTradesPerDay = 5 is an arbitrary placeholder default, flagged for calibration.

Needs a trade-count-since-period-start accessor that does not currently exist in the corpus; closest existing tool is LastTradeCooldown's use of TotalTrades, which is a lifetime counter, not a per-day/week/month one.
